item.title: Refinements to precision-information imputation in meta-analysis of survival rates: Boundary correction and cross-study borrowing
item.description: arXiv:2611.33600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Meta-analyses of survival rates require precision information, such as standard errors (SEs), which is often unreported. We previously proposed imputing missing SEs from reported survival rates, sample sizes, and risk-set sizes. The original method has two limitations. First, it replaces Kaplan--Meier estimates of 1 with 0.99 regardless of sample size. Second, when the risk-set size is unavailable, it uses the total event count as a fallback. The count is often unreported, and the fallback can also substantially overestimate SEs. We propose a sample-size-dependent boundary correction based on a pseudo-event and a method that borrows time-specific event information from studies with available risk-set sizes. In simulations, the boundary correction was more stable than fixed replacement, and borrowing reduced study-level SE imputation bias. Borrowing generally improved precision by retaining studies with missing SEs that lacked both risk-set sizes and event counts.
item.dc:creator: Kazushi Maruo, Yusuke Yamaguchi, Ryota Ishii, Hisashi Noma, Masahiko Gosho

item.title: Cutting Bus Service Without Cutting Access: Persistent Homology of Service Deserts and Timetable Reductions
item.description: arXiv:2611.33659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Japanese bus operators are withdrawing service for lack of drivers, and the choice of which trips to withdraw determines who keeps a bus. We measure service at each stop from vehicle GPS and smart-card records, without timetables, and use persistent homology of walking and walking-plus-waiting time to find enclosed service deserts: pockets surrounded by service but beyond walking distance from it. Around Tsukuba, 35 such pockets lie more than 800m from any station or hourly stop. The 17 that are fully ringed by walkable service hold 18,446 residents. We compare two 2020 timetable reductions by Kanto Railway with random reductions and a heuristic frontier of same-size, capacity-feasible alternatives. At two and four buses an hour, both reductions protected service better than random reductions. No alternative found by the sweep dominates the state-of-emergency timetable. The summer timetable is dominated: it withdrew hourly service from 5,253 residents around stops with almost no morning riders, whereas same-size alternatives kept it for all of them at equal waiting. Averages hide a tail: under the actual timetables, 5.9% and 3.9% of residents are at stops whose expected wait rises by 10 minutes or more, against 0.5% and 0.3% in the alternatives, and capping the increase at 10 minutes at every served stop is feasible at the operator's sizes. If half the removed hours become paid hours saved, the labor saving of both reductions and their main alternatives fall short of the fare revenue on the removed trips.
item.dc:creator: Fabiana Ferracina, Ayane Nakmura, Bala Krishnamoorthy, Hiroyasu Ando

item.title: Shooting for Fit: Risk-Averse Stochastic Roster Construction from Bayesian Shot-Pattern Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.33820v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Roster construction is a critical decision problem in professional basketball, requiring teams to balance player quality, player complementarity, and financial constraints under uncertainty. Existing roster optimization models primarily rely on individual player ratings and aggregate performance statistics, which provide limited information about how players' offensive contributions vary with their teammates. Recent advances in player-tracking technology have enabled statistical analyses of spatial shooting patterns, but these insights have rarely informed roster construction. We bridge this gap by developing a data-driven, risk-averse two-stage stochastic optimization framework for NBA roster construction. We first develop a Bayesian modeling framework that combines player statistics and spatial shot-chart data to identify player roles and estimate how teammate composition influences shot selection, shooting frequency, and scoring efficiency. The resulting model provides uncertainty-quantified offensive values for hypothetical five-player lineups, including combinations that have never played together. We then formulate roster construction as a two-stage stochastic mixed-integer program that optimizes player acquisitions under NBA salary-cap regulations while allowing lineup playing-time allocations to adapt to uncertain player roles. We evaluate the framework using 240 team-offseason decisions over eight seasons and two additional held-out seasons. The results demonstrate that incorporating spatial shooting compatibility substantially changes optimal roster decisions and improves predicted offensive performance relative to approaches based on individual player values. We further find that flexibility in allocating playing time across lineups absorbs much of the uncertainty about player roles.
item.dc:creator: Yue Yu, Cong Zhang, David Crandall, Guanyu Hu

item.title: The Illusion of an Automated German Census: Assessing the Feasibility of the 2031 Register-Based Census via Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The next German Census (2031) is planned to be the country's first fully register-based census, relying exclusively on administrative data sources. In addition to the population registers, ten further administrative registers are envisaged, covering a wide range of information, from driving licences to agricultural social insurance. This study simulates potential data-quality challenges in linking these registers using quasi-identifiers (QIDs), such as names and dates of birth. Using a synthetic population dataset (N=80,206,770), we systematically vary experimental factors related to register characteristics. Across the 1,458 experimental conditions studied, results vary considerably. Some plausible scenarios range from 500,000 to 1,000,000 false-negative linkage errors per linked register. These findings suggest that implementing an automated register-based census using the currently envisaged registers may prove challenging and could require substantial manual post-processing to achieve acceptable data quality.
item.dc:creator: R. Schnell (University of Duisburg-Essen), S. V. Weiand (University of Duisburg-Essen)

item.title: A new method of Ecological Inference based on the Cressie--Read power divergence
item.description: arXiv:2611.34070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ecological inference aims to estimate the bivariate association structure between a pair of variables from the row and column totals of a set of contingency tables. The paper introduces a new approach based on minimizing the Cressie--Read power divergence, applied to the estimation of vote transitions between two elections. It also outlines a Fisher scoring algorithm and derives the asymptotic distribution of the estimator.
item.dc:creator: Jose M. Pav\'ia, Antonio Forcina

item.title: When precision exceeds fidelity: systematic error quantification for inference with misspecified simulators
item.description: arXiv:2611.33282v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As scientific datasets grow in complexity and precision, the primary source of uncertainty in parameter inference shifts from measurement noise to systematic errors within the simulators themselves. In this setting, Bayesian evidence concentrates on whichever misspecified model best approximates the data. Evidence-weighted model averaging can then underestimate systematic uncertainty when one model component compensates for the misspecification of another component. We posit that in this case, the key question is how each model responds to discrepancies between simulator and data. We show that the local response of an inferred parameter to perturbations in the data --- the model's influence map --- can be estimated efficiently from forward evaluations of the simulator at existing posterior samples. Propagating discrepancy residuals through these influence maps enables individual sources of systematic bias to be isolated. Applied to independent observations used to infer the mass of a supermassive black hole, we find that the error is dominated by model systematics. We identify a simplification shared by all models, propagate the discrepancies through each model's influence map, and apply a first-order correction of the resulting biases. This substantially improves the cross-observation consistency of the inferred black-hole mass within each model while preserving the between-model spread that represents remaining systematics.
item.dc:creator: M. J. Yantovski-Barth, Hengyue Zhang, Nolan Smyth, Aristeidis Amvrosiadis, Martin Bureau, Yashar Hezaveh, Laurence Perreault-Levasseur

item.title: A Quantile-Based Framework for Bimodal Distribution Construction
item.description: arXiv:2611.33329v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study suggests a novel quantile-based framework to construct bimodal distribution which does not rely on mixture representations or closed-form probability density functions. This proposed approach induces bimodality by transforming the quantile density through a strictly positive modulation function so that it can preserve the support and tail behavior of a chosen baseline distribution with providing explicit control over modal structure. The method is shown to apply broadly across bounded, semi-bounded and unbounded distribution families which include power, reflected power, logistic, Weibull and generalized lambda distributions. Simulation studies and a real-data application were performed which have shown that the proposed construction yields smooth, interpretable and computationally stable bimodal models and it also provides a flexible alternative to classical mixture-based approaches. Also this framework allows gradual transitions between unimodal and bimodal shapes which make it well suited for modeling overlapping regimes which are commonly encountered in real-world data. This proposed methodology therefor offers a robust and interpretable tool for bimodal modeling without requiring latent class assumptions or complex estimation procedures.
item.dc:creator: Dreamlee Sharma, Nikita Rawat

item.title: APEX: Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration
item.description: arXiv:2611.33450v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ensemble-based methods provide a practical framework for history matching, prediction, and optimization of subsurface models. In methodological studies, however, performance is rarely assessed from a single run. Comparisons typically span cases, configurations, and random seeds, while each evaluation may require an expensive external simulator. Keeping such studies computationally bounded, auditable, and reproducible therefore requires more than implementing a numerical method: experiments must be validated before execution, computational costs estimated, repeated runs organized consistently, and configurations and outputs made traceable. To address these needs, we developed APEX (Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration), an open-source Python platform that provides a common framework for configuring, validating, executing, recording, and comparing ensemble-based experiments. APEX is organized around three concepts: an experiment defines what is executed, a run records a single execution, and a study coordinates and compares multiple experiments or runs. Experiments are specified through validated configurations, which can also be generated by a planner agent. Before execution, APEX estimates the maximum number of forward simulations required. If the estimate exceeds a user-defined threshold, submission is held for approval. Each run records provenance information, while studies repeat problems across variants and paired replicates and compare results using paired statistical analyses. Scientific and computational components, including methods, simulators, metrics, and optimizers, are implemented as plugins. A command line interface, Python client, REST service with a web interface, and tools for language model agents access these capabilities through a common service layer.
item.dc:creator: Xiaodong Luo

item.title: Simple, general strategies for correcting the upward bias of calibration summaries of prediction models
item.description: arXiv:2611.33846v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For clinical prediction models, calibration across the spectrum of predicted values is often assessed via flexible calibration curves and associated scalar summaries such as the integrated calibration index (ICI). However, these scalar summaries tend to have a finite-sample upward bias, as they are based on the absolute value of an estimate whose sampling distribution can cross zero. We show the mechanism underlying this bias and quantify its magnitude as a function of the true calibration error and its variance. This mechanism motivates easily implementable methods for reducing the bias (plug-in and inversion methods, each applied locally or globally) that are applicable to any smoothing method that generates an estimate and its sampling variance for each point on the calibration curve. These methods are general in that 1) they can be used for different outcome types (continuous, binary, time-to-event, as well as counterfactual outcomes for models that predict treatment benefit), and 2) the resulting bias-adjusted calibration error curves yield bias-corrected estimates of other metrics such as quantile-based ones (e.g., E50 and E90). Focusing on ICI as an exemplary metric, numerical and case studies demonstrate that the upward bias can be substantial, especially when the sample is small and the true ICI is close to zero. Results show that the Global Inversion method removed the most bias, particularly when the bias was substantial, although it could slightly increase the mean absolute error if the bias was small.
item.dc:creator: Mohsen Sadatsafavi, Ramin Rezaeianzadeh, Hessam Sadatsafavi

item.title: Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Models for Predicting Donor Kidney Discard
item.description: arXiv:2602.21876v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A kidney transplant can significantly improve the life expectancy and quality of life of patients with end-stage renal failure. Even more patients could be helped with a kidney transplant if the rate of kidneys that are discarded and not transplanted could be reduced. Machine learning (ML) techniques can support decision-making in this context by early identification of donor organs at high risk of discard. Although various ML models have been applied, their results are difficult to compare due to heterogenous datasets and differences in feature engineering and evaluation strategies. This study aims to provide a systematic and reproducible comparison of ML models for donor-level kidney discard prediction. We trained five ML models: Logistic Regression (LR), Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting (GB), and Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) along with an ensemble model on data from 4,080 deceased donors in Germany. We implemented a benchmarking framework, including standardized feature engineering, supervised feature selection, and Bayesian hyperparameter optimization. Model performance was assessed for discrimination, calibration, and explainability. The ensemble achieved the highest discrimination performance. However, the results did not differ significantly from those of LR. Individual models such as LR, RF, and MLP performed comparably and substantially better than DT. Platt scaling generally improved calibration. SHAP identified age and renal markers as dominant predictors across models, reflecting clinical plausibility. This study demonstrates that consistent data preprocessing, feature selection, and evaluation can be more decisive for predictive success than the choice of the ML algorithm. The proposed benchmarking framework enables transparent comparison of models and provides a reproducible foundation for improving donor-level kidney discard prediction.
item.dc:creator: Peer Schliephacke, Hannah Schult, Leon Mizera, Judith W\"urfel, Gunter Grieser, Axel Rahmel, Carl-Ludwig Fischer-Fr\"ohlich, Antje Jahn-Eimermacher

item.title: Critique of "Use of roster charts in the investigation and prosecution of nurses ..." by John O'Quigley
item.description: arXiv:2606.29394v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The paper "Use of roster charts in the investigation and prosecution of nurses suspected of inflicting deliberate harm on patients" by Prof. John O'Quigley explores an interesting hypothesis concerning statistical information hidden in the part of the infamous Lucy Letby roster chart pertaining to the 37 other nurses. Unfortunately, we have to point out some serious errors in his statistical analyses. The data actually contains information which strongly disproves his main modelling assumption. We do, however, strongly agree with him that from a forensic statistical point of view, the roster chart is fake evidence which should not have been shown to jurors.
item.dc:creator: Richard D. Gill

item.title: Estimating Distributions with Failure Rate Properties from Noisy Quantile Data
item.description: arXiv:2607.13212v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Estimating an unknown cumulative distribution function (cdf) is fundamental both as a statistical goal and as an input to downstream optimization. In practice, however, distribution estimation is often complicated by incomplete knowledge of the distribution's structure and limited, censored data. We address the first challenge by studying distributions with failure-rate shape constraints, especially increasing failure rate (IFR), without assuming a fully specified parametric family. To address the second, we consider noisy quantile data: at finitely many prespecified knots, each observation records only whether an independent sample lies below or above the knot. This setting arises naturally in pricing, reliability, and healthcare. We formulate the IFR-constrained maximum likelihood estimator and show that the original problem is infinite-dimensional and non-convex. Our two-step approach solves a finite-dimensional convex optimization problem over transformed knot values, then reconstructs a full cdf through shape-preserving interpolation. We establish finite-sample error bounds and convergence rates that guide offline data collection. We also show how the framework accommodates additional properties: (i) decreasing failure rate, (ii) failure rate average, (iii) generalized failure rate, and (iv) new better than used. Numerical experiments and case studies in revenue management and reliability illustrate improved goodness of fit and downstream decision quality.
item.dc:creator: Timothy C. Y. Chan, Ningyuan Chen, Craig Fernandes, Muhammad Maaz

item.title: Evaluating laser scanning data sources, canopy metrics, and predictor resolution for forest inventory
item.description: arXiv:2610.06476v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Forest managers updating growing stock volume (GSV) estimates must decide whether existing LiDAR data calibrated with current inventory are sufficient or a new acquisition provides worthwhile improvements. We compared regional airborne laser scanning (ALS) acquired in 2023 with uncrewed aerial vehicle laser scanning (ULS) from 2026 in a mixed-species forest in north-eastern Germany. Both datasets were calibrated using the same 2026 personal laser scanning inventory within a change-of-support regression framework. We compared 3 m and 35 m grids, canopy height alone and with three structural metrics, and models with and without spatial random effects. Evaluation comprised 10-fold cross-validation (CV) on 118 undisturbed plots (no tree removal), prediction on 33 disturbed plots (detected removal) excluded from calibration, and CV across all 151 plots. In undisturbed CV, the lowest root mean squared prediction errors (RMSPEs) were 74.1 m3 ha-1 for ULS and 81.5 m3 ha-1 for ALS, a 9.1% reduction for ULS. Both used spatial effects and 3 m predictors, with structural metrics for ULS and canopy height only for ALS. At 3 m, canopy-height-only models performed similarly across sources, whereas adding structural metrics improved ULS predictions. Finer grids improved both sources, and spatial effects gave only small gains. On the disturbed holdout, 3 m ULS models had little bias, whereas ALS overpredicted volume, consistent with predictors representing pre-removal conditions. Canopy-height-only ULS outperformed the four-predictor models on these plots. Across all 151 plots, the 3 m four-predictor ULS models achieved an RMSPE of 70.5 m3 ha-1 versus 81.5 m3 ha-1 for the best ALS model, a 13.5% reduction. Existing ALS therefore retained substantial predictive value on undisturbed plots, while ULS provided additional information and supported estimation across both disturbance classes.

item.title: United in Diversity? Contextual Biases in LLM-Based Predictions of the 2024 European Parliament Elections
item.description: arXiv:2409.09045v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: "Silicon samples" based on large language models (LLMs) have been argued to serve as efficient alternatives to surveys of humans, assuming that their training data includes information on human attitudes and behavior. However, LLM-generated survey data might exhibit biases, for example due to a lack of diversity in training and alignment processes, which risk reinforcing existing biases in research and policymaking. In this study, we examine to what extent LLM-based predictions of individual public opinion exhibit context-dependent biases by predicting the results of the 2024 EU elections. Before the elections have taken place, we prompt three LLMs with individual-level background information of 26,000 eligible European voters to predict each person's voting behavior. We show that when compared to the actual results, LLM-based predictions of future voting behavior largely fail, their accuracy is unequally distributed across national and linguistic contexts, and they require detailed attitudinal information in the prompt. The findings emphasize the limited applicability of silicon samples to public opinion prediction. In investigating their contextual biases, this study contributes to the understanding and mitigation of inequalities in the development of LLMs and their applications in computational social science.
item.dc:creator: Leah von der Heyde, Anna-Carolina Haensch, Alexander Wenz, Bolei Ma

item.title: Bayesian Instrumented Directed Graphical Models for Cyclic Causal Discovery with Unmeasured Confounding
item.description: arXiv:2510.09991v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In networks with feedback, a pairwise instrumental-variable estimate can combine direct and indirect effects. We propose a Bayesian cyclic structural equation model with spike-and-slab priors on direct effects and on error covariances representing unmeasured confounding. Its joint posterior quantifies support for edges, confounding links, and feedback loops. The model has two versions. IV-RGM takes as known the map that lists which responses each instrument affects directly. IV-RGM+ learns this map. A rank condition identifies the model with a known map. For an unknown map, we give conditions on instrument effects and cycle gains that identify the representation with the fewest direct instrument effects. We establish posterior consistency and directed graph recovery under additional conditions. In smaller simulated samples with strong instruments, IV-RGM ranked direct edges more accurately than competing methods when the map was correct. When the supplied map omitted shared targets, IV-RGM+ ranked edges most accurately and reduced false discoveries relative to fixing the incorrect map. Weak instruments limited recovery across methods. In B cells, the analysis with a known map gave limited support to feedback among inhibitory receptor genes. Both versions are available in an R package on CRAN (https://cran.r-project.org/package=MR.RGM).
item.dc:creator: Bitan Sarkar, Yuchao Jiang, Tian Ge, Yang Ni

item.title: Design-Conditional Prior Elicitation for Dirichlet Process Mixtures: A Unified Framework for Cluster Counts and Weight Control
item.description: arXiv:2602.06301v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dirichlet process mixtures (DPMs) model variation in effects across sites or studies and in latent traits among examinees. The concentration parameter affects both the number of clusters in the sample and the population weights, yet its hyperprior is often chosen by default. We describe a method for choosing this hyperprior when the number of units is fixed by design. We calibrate a Gamma hyperprior to the analyst's expected cluster count and uncertainty about it, then examine the implied weights. If count and weight judgments conflict, Dual-Anchor selects a compromise and reports its implications for both. Across our simulations and applications, the choice of prior could change the inferred number of clusters considerably even when individual estimates changed little. A higher cluster count under an alternative prior warrants a closer look at the upper tail, where estimates can shift even when the median remains stable. The DPprior R package implements the calibration and diagnostics.
item.dc:creator: JoonHo Lee

item.title: Distribution-Free Changepoint Inference for Rainfall Patterns
item.description: arXiv:2609.13594v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long records of rainfall contain critical information about the temporal organization of precipitation within a year, including wet and dry spells. Detecting when this temporal pattern changes is central to climate-impact assessment and environmental monitoring.A common data structure features observations from m locations over T years. For location i and year t, the record is a vector of daily measurements $X_{i,t} = (X_{i,t,1}, ..., X_{i,t,D})^\top$, with D = 365. The goal is to identify an unknown year $t_0$ when the temporal rainfall pattern changes across the region. Because changes in the intra-annual pattern affect the frequency-domain behavior of the daily sequence, we represent each yearly curve through a spectral feature capturing the strength of temporal oscillation at a fixed frequency.Classical changepoint methods often rely on parametric likelihoods or Gaussian approximations, which are hard to justify for skewed and heavy-tailed rainfall data. Furthermore, many procedures only return a point estimate. A confidence set for the change year is crucial in environmental applications to quantify temporal uncertainty and distinguish sharp transitions from weak evidence.This paper develops a distribution-free framework for detecting a synchronized structural change in yearly rainfall patterns across independently monitored locations. For each location-year pair, we compute a fixed-frequency nonparametric spectral density estimate. These features form a $T \times m$ data matrix. By exploiting the exchangeability of yearly spectral features before and after the true changepoint, alongside spatial independence, we construct finite-sample valid confidence sets for the unknown change year.
item.dc:creator: Aaditya Jain (Abstract Math Institute), Abhishek Bhattacharjee (Abstract Math Institute)

item.title: Extreme Binary Classification: Extreme Value Theory for Extreme Constraint on False Negative
item.description: arXiv:2610.09984v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While binary classification is one of the most extensively studied problems in machine learning, the regime in which the goal is to learn a classifier with an almost zero false negative rate remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce the Extreme Binary Classification problem, where the objective is to learn a classifier whose false negative rate $\alpha$ is constrained by $\epsilon_{N_1}=o_{N_1\to\infty}(1/N_1)$, with $N_1$ denoting the number of positive examples in the training set. To address this problem, we propose a threshold adaptation method theoretically grounded in guarantees derived from Extreme Value Theory, together with a feature selection procedure based on a permutation test applied to sample maxima. Experimental results on four real-world datasets of varying sizes demonstrate that our approach compares favorably with state-of-the-art methods. In addition, we illustrate its interpretability through an application to a cancer screening dataset.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Gruffaz, Muhammad Fawad, Jaakko Nevalainen

item.title: Functional nestedness of soil nematode communities across Europe: integrating morphological counts and eDNA reads
item.description: arXiv:2611.18819v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: 1. Soil nematodes occupy multiple trophic positions and contribute to key processes in soil food webs. Their communities vary across land uses and environmental conditions, yet it remains unclear whether these differences mainly reflect taxon replacement or nested patterns of taxon occurrence. 2. Here, we analysed two independent European datasets of soil nematode communities, SOB4ES, based on eDNA metabarcoding, and NemEu, based on morphological identification, to examine how genus composition varies across land uses. We partitioned community dissimilarity into turnover and nestedness-resultant components and compared sites under contrasting land uses with those sharing the same land use, while accounting for geographical and soil-related variation. We also assessed matrix-level nestedness, differences among trophic groups and associations between genus composition and environmental gradients. 3. In both datasets, genus turnover was consistently greater between contrasting land uses than within the same land use. Although the differences were modest, they remained significant after accounting for geographical distance and genus richness, whereas nestedness-resultant dissimilarity contributed little to land-use differentiation. These findings suggest that land-use-associated differences in European nematode communities are expressed primarily through changes in genus identity rather than nested patterns of taxon occurrence. 4. The consistency of this result across independently assembled datasets supports the broader relevance of taxonomic turnover for understanding soil biodiversity patterns across European land uses.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Nicolosi, Michael Bonkowski, Carlo Febbi, Christian Mulder

item.title: Bayesian Computation of Copula-based Multivariate Models with an Application to Doping Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.24801v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Athlete Biological Passport (ABP) monitors athletes for doping by comparing their biomarker readings against personalized reference ranges. These are estimated via the Bayesian ADAPTIVE model, which analyzes biomarkers separately and ignores their dependence. Building on a recently proposed copula-based multivariate extension of ADAPTIVE, this paper focuses on its computational aspects, introducing a fully joint MCMC algorithm and comparing it with a two-step Bayesian IFM estimator. Simulations show the two procedures perform comparably under a correctly specified copula, but exhibit a genuine trade-off under misspecification: the Bayesian IFM protects marginal inference, while the joint MCMC yields better-calibrated dependence estimates and is markedly faster. The two approaches are tested on a dataset containing ABP profiles of elite athletes, provided by NADO Italia, and collected as part of the project "Enhancing the methodological framework for doping detection: from univariate to multivariate testing analysis on Athlete Biological Passport profiles". Both approaches achieve consistent classification performance, providing anti-doping organizations with two concrete inferential routes for adopting a multivariate ADAPTIVE model, along with guidance on the trade-offs between them.
item.dc:creator: Emanuele Masillo, Pigi-Eva Vyltanioti, Nina Deliu, Brunero Liseo
